title: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus: Autoimmunity, Organ Manifestations and Belimumab

content.intro: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) has a rich and fascinating history that spans over two centuries. The disease was first described by Hippocrates in 400 BCE, but it wasn't until 1828 that the French physician Pierre Cazenave coined the term 'lupus erythematosus'. In 1872, the Austrian dermatologist Moritz Kaposi described the characteristic butterfly-shaped rash on the face, which is now a hallmark of the disease. The 20th century saw significant advancements in the understanding of SLE, with the discovery of the lupus erythematosus cell in 1948 by Malcolm Hargraves and the introduction of corticosteroids as a treatment in the 1950s. The 1980s saw the development of the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) criteria for the classification of SLE, which has undergone several revisions since then. In 2011, the US FDA approved belimumab, a monoclonal antibody that targets the BLyS protein, for the treatment of SLE. Famous cases of SLE include the actress Selena Gomez, who has been open about her struggles with the disease.

content.intro: SLE is a complex autoimmune disease characterized by the production of autoantibodies against various nuclear and cytoplasmic components. The exact aetiology of SLE is still not fully understood, but it is believed to involve a combination of genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors. Molecular mechanisms involved in the pathogenesis of SLE include the activation of immune cells, the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, and the deposition of immune complexes in tissues. Genetic factors, such as mutations in the IRF5 and STAT4 genes, have been identified as risk factors for SLE. Subtypes of SLE include cutaneous lupus, systemic lupus, and lupus nephritis. The role of epigenetics and the gut microbiome in the development of SLE is an area of active research.

content.intro: The clinical presentation of SLE can vary widely, but common symptoms include fever, fatigue, joint pain, and skin rashes. The characteristic butterfly-shaped rash on the face is present in approximately 50% of patients. Other symptoms may include hair loss, mouth ulcers, and photosensitivity. SLE can affect various organs, including the kidneys, lungs, heart, and brain. Cardinal symptoms of SLE include the presence of autoantibodies, such as anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA), and the presence of at least four of the ACR criteria. Atypical presentations of SLE may include isolated organ involvement, such as lupus nephritis or neuropsychiatric SLE. The disease can be divided into stages, including a preclinical stage, an active stage, and a quiescent stage.

content.intro: The diagnosis of SLE is a complex process that requires a combination of clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings. The ACR and SLICC criteria provide a framework for diagnosis, but it is essential to consider the individual patient's presentation and medical history. Laboratory tests, such as ANA and anti-dsDNA antibody assays, are crucial for diagnosis, while imaging studies may be used to evaluate organ involvement. Differential diagnosis is also essential to rule out other autoimmune diseases. The development of new biomarkers and diagnostic tests is ongoing, and these advances are expected to improve the diagnosis and monitoring of SLE.

content.intro: The treatment of SLE is tailored to the individual patient's needs, depending on the severity and organ involvement. Non-pharmacological interventions, such as lifestyle modifications and patient education, are essential for managing SLE. Pharmacological treatments, including NSAIDs, antimalarials, and corticosteroids, are used to control symptoms and prevent organ damage. Immunosuppressive agents and biologic agents, such as belimumab, may be used to treat severe or refractory SLE. A multidisciplinary approach is necessary to optimize outcomes in SLE patients, and regular monitoring and adjustments to treatment are crucial to achieve the best possible results.

content.intro: SLE is associated with a range of complications, which can significantly impact the quality of life and prognosis of patients. The incidence of complications varies depending on the population and disease severity, and prognostic scores can be used to predict outcomes. While the prognosis of SLE has improved significantly over the past few decades, the disease remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality. Early recognition and treatment of complications are essential to improve outcomes, and ongoing research is focused on developing new treatments and improving our understanding of the underlying mechanisms of SLE complications.

content.intro: SLE is a complex disease that requires special consideration in different populations, including children, the elderly, and pregnant women. Emerging therapies, including biologic agents and small molecule inhibitors, offer promising opportunities for improving outcomes in SLE patients. However, further research is needed to fully understand the safety and efficacy of these new therapies. The development of personalized treatment approaches, tailored to the individual patient's needs, is an area of ongoing research. Special consideration is needed for SLE patients with comorbidities, and international collaboration and knowledge sharing are essential to advance our understanding of SLE and improve outcomes for patients worldwide.
